title: The Odyssey IMAX Tickets Just Went Live in India. The Price Map Is Wild.
excerpt: Christopher Nolan's first film shot entirely on IMAX cameras opened advance booking today — ₹370 in Delhi, ₹3,000 in Pune, and scalpers asking thousands of dollars in New York.
body:
At exactly 10:00 AM on June 8, India became one of the first countries in the world to open advance booking for **Christopher Nolan**'s **The Odyssey** — and within hours, the ticket price map had turned into its own Greek drama. In Pune, a single IMAX seat for the evening show is selling for ₹3,000. In Delhi, at Inox Paras, you can walk in for ₹370. Same film. Same IMAX. Same Christopher Nolan. Eight times the price difference.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=Mzw2ttJD2qQ</youtube>

This isn't *Oppenheimer* pricing, which already felt like a stretch in 2023. This is something new — the first time in cinema history that a film shot entirely on IMAX cameras has gone on sale, and the market is treating it like a luxury product launch rather than a movie ticket.

The numbers tell the story. **Mumbai** runs the full spectrum: Inox Malad is keeping morning shows at a civilised ₹450–520, while Cinepolis Seawoods has no ticket under ₹1,300, with evening slots touching ₹2,000. **Pune** takes the crown for India's most expensive IMAX seat — Cinepolis Aundh and Inox Megaplex are charging up to ₹3,000 for prime evening slots. **Delhi**, meanwhile, is the accidental hero: Inox Paras has listed its morning show from ₹370 to ₹490, making it arguably the cheapest way to see a Nolan film in IMAX anywhere on the planet right now.

**Bengaluru** sits in the middle at ₹900–1,000. **Kochi** ranges from ₹750 to ₹950. **Coimbatore**'s Broadway has gone with a pleasantly weird flat rate of ₹508 — because nothing says premium cinema like pricing that looks like a petrol bill. And **Kolkata**'s Inox South City starts at ₹470 for the early bird.

> "The Odyssey is the first film in cinema history to be shot entirely on IMAX cameras, a milestone Christopher Nolan spent nearly twenty years working toward." — Denzil Dias, VP & Managing Director, Warner Bros. Discovery India

Globally, the situation is even wilder. When IMAX tickets went live in the US, platforms buckled under the traffic. Apps crashed. Queues stretched into thousands. Scalpers swooped in instantly — on eBay, three tickets to a 70MM IMAX screening at New York's Lincoln Square sold for a combined $700. Unsold listings are asking thousands per seat. The problem is supply: there are only **39 theatres worldwide** capable of showing the film in 70MM IMAX, with 24 of them in the United States. Each venue has one equipped screen and can manage four or five shows a day. For a film with a nearly three-hour runtime, every seat is a hot commodity.

The cast alone would justify the frenzy. **Matt Damon** leads as Odysseus, with **Tom Holland** as his son Telemachus and **Anne Hathaway** as Penelope. Then there's **Zendaya**, **Robert Pattinson**, **Lupita Nyong'o**, **Charlize Theron**, and **Jon Bernthal** — the kind of lineup that makes the film feel less like a movie and more like a civilisational event. Nolan directing Homer's ancient Greek epic with this cast and this format is the most ambitious thing happening in cinema this year, and possibly this decade.

For the **Indian diaspora**, the ticketing chaos cuts both ways. If you're in the US, you're competing with the entire country for 24 IMAX 70mm screens — good luck if you're not near New York, LA, or San Francisco. If you're planning a trip back to India this summer, the math becomes absurd: you could fly to Delhi, catch *The Odyssey* at Inox Paras for ₹370, eat a full dinner at a nice restaurant, and still spend less than a scalper's single ticket in Manhattan.

India is also getting the film day-and-date on **July 17, 2026**, across all formats — standard screens, premium large format, and IMAX. The smart play for NRIs who don't want to fight the American ticket wars: book in India now, plan the family visit around it, and tell everyone at the next dinner party that you saw Nolan's magnum opus in IMAX for the price of a coffee at Starbucks.

There's a deeper story here, too. India's IMAX screen count has been quietly expanding — and Nolan knows it. His decision to allow India advance sales on the same day as the US isn't charity. It's recognition that the Indian market has become a serious IMAX audience, one that turned *Oppenheimer* into a cultural moment and made *Dhurandhar: The Revenge* break IMAX records earlier this year. Warner Bros. Discovery treating Indian fans as equals in the booking queue is new, and it's significant.

The film opens July 17. The IMAX seats are filling now. And somewhere between a ₹370 ticket in Delhi and a $700 scalper listing in New York, Christopher Nolan just proved that the future of cinema runs on a different price map depending on which city you wake up in.
